result.instructions: Linkz draws vector art written in lizard-script. Call docs first to learn the language and the drawing functions, write the code, check it with run, then look at it with render and improve it. Save finished work with save.

tools.name: docs
tools.description: Start here. Explains how to draw in Linkz by writing lizard-script (canvas, layers, points, colors, gradients, blend modes, pens) and lists every drawing function with its parameters, a summary and an example. With name, gives the full documentation of that one function.

name.description: A function name, like circle or linear. Leave out for the primer and the whole list.

tools.name: run
tools.description: Runs lizard-script drawing code and reports {ok, errors: [{line, column, message}], printed, shapes, steps, ms} as JSON, without drawing a picture. Use it to check code quickly.

code.description: The lizard-script source of the drawing (the contents of a .lzdraw file).

tools.name: render
tools.description: Runs the drawing code and returns the picture as a PNG image, so you can see what you drew (plus the errors, if there were any). Width and height scale the picture to fit, keeping its shape.

code.description: The lizard-script source of the drawing (the contents of a .lzdraw file).

width.description: Fit the picture in this many pixels across.

height.description: Fit the picture in this many pixels high.

tools.name: svg
tools.description: Runs the drawing code and returns the drawing as SVG text.

code.description: The lizard-script source of the drawing (the contents of a .lzdraw file).

tools.name: save
tools.description: Writes the code as a .lzdraw file. A relative path goes in the user's drawings folder (settings.drawings_dir, by default ~/Documents/Linkz); an absolute path must be inside the home folder. It never replaces a file unless overwrite is true.

path.description: File name or path, like sunset.lzdraw. .lzdraw is added when there is no extension.

code.description: The lizard-script source of the drawing (the contents of a .lzdraw file).

overwrite.description: Replace the file if it exists. Default false.

tools.name: trace
tools.description: Traces a picture file (.png, .jpg or .jpeg, inside the user's home or drawings folder) into drawing code. Returns three items: the generated .lzdraw code (text), the stats as JSON (text) and a PNG render of the traced drawing, so you can compare it with the original and trace again with other settings. Mode "lineart" traces inked line art (pen drawings, sketches, comics) into strokes and fills instead of color regions. Pass the code to run, render or save to keep working on it. Slow for big pictures: lower max_side.

path.description: The image file: an absolute path inside the home folder, ~/..., or a path relative to the drawings folder.

colors.description: How many colors the drawing may use. Default 8.

detail.description: How closely outlines follow the picture; higher keeps more. Default 1.5.

max_side.description: The picture is shrunk until its longer side is at most this many pixels. Default 256.

min_area.description: Regions smaller than this many pixels are merged into a neighbour. Default 8.

corner.description: The turn in degrees from which an outline point stays a sharp corner. Default 55.

background.description: Write the biggest color as one rectangle behind everything. Default true (photo mode).

mode.description: photo (default) traces color regions; lineart traces ink lines as strokes and the areas between them as fills.

line_threshold.description: Lineart: how much darker than its surroundings a pixel must be to start a line, 0 to 1; lower finds fainter lines. Default 0.5.

line_min.description: Lineart: strokes shorter than this many pixels (length plus width) are dropped. Default 6.

continuation.description: Lineart: the largest turn in degrees a line may make at a junction and still go on as the same stroke. Default 35.

radius.description: Lineart: half side in pixels of the neighbourhood a pixel is compared with; 0 picks it from the picture size. Default 0.

fills.description: Lineart: false to trace only the lines, on the paper color. Default true.

solid.description: Lineart: ink at least this many pixels from the paper all round is a solid fill, not a stroke; 0 picks it from the size. Default 0.

quality.description: Lineart: a preset of options. light: smaller code, a little more error; balanced: the defaults; detailed: more colors and tighter outlines (about 2x the code); max: detailed on a picture up to 1600 px (slow, big); auto: traces light, balanced and detailed in parallel, scores each against the picture and keeps the best (the stats say which, under picked). Options given too win over the preset. Implies mode lineart.

box.description: [x, y, w, h] in pixels of the picture at its own size.

detail.description: Above 1 for more detail, below 1 for less. Default 2.

focus.description: Lineart: boxes where the trace should have more detail (detail above 1) or less (below 1), for example [{"box": [40, 30, 60, 60], "detail": 2}].

tools.name: open
tools.description: Reads a .lzdraw file and returns its code. Same path rules as save.

path.description: File name or path of the .lzdraw.

content.text:
# Drawing in Linkz

A Linkz drawing is a lizard-script program (a .lzdraw file). Never write SVG: write code that calls the drawing functions below, then use the render tool to look at the result and fix what is wrong.

## The basics
- A line starting with -~> is a comment. Saved files start with the line `-~> lzdraw 1`.
- Set the canvas first: `canvas = {"size": (480, 320), "background": #f6d9a8}`. The default is 512 by 512 and white.
- Points are `(x, y)`: x grows to the right, y grows DOWN, (0, 0) is the top-left corner. Points add and scale: `p + (10, 5)`, `p * 2`, and `p.x`, `p.y` read a coordinate.
- Colors: `#3fa34d`, `#rgb`, `#rrggbbaa` (the last two digits are the alpha), `rgb(r, g, b)`, `rgba(r, g, b, a)`, `hsl(h, s, l)` (degrees, percent, percent).
- Every shape call draws and also returns the shape, so `let c = circle((100, 100), 30, #3fa34d)` lets you change it later with `c.fill = #e0a526`.
- Shapes: circle, ellipse, rect, line, polygon, stroke (a smooth curve through points), brush (a pressure-sensitive stroke). See the function list for their parameters.
- Units: `45deg`, `0.25turn`, `10px`. `math.sin`, `math.cos`, `math.pi`, `math.random()` (the same numbers on every run) are there, like the `text` and `list` helpers.
- The language: `let x = 1`, `x = x + 1`, `x += 1`; `if (c) { } elif (d) { } else { }`; `for (let i = 0; i < 6; i = i + 1) { }`; `while (c) { }`; `function f(a, b = 2) { a + b }`; lists `[1, 2]` and hashes `{"k": v}`; `try { } catch (e) { puts(e.message) }`; `puts(...)` prints (you get it back in `printed`).

## Layers
A layer is the word `layer`, a name, and an indented body (indent the body deeper than the word `layer`, with 2 spaces):

    layer sun
      circle((360, 90), 34, #fff3c4)
    layer sky
      rect((0, 0), (480, 320), #f2a65a)

Layers higher in the file are IN FRONT of the ones below, and inside a layer the objects higher up are in front too. So write the foreground first and the background last (the opposite of most drawing programs). Layers nest. Inside a layer, `blend("multiply")` mixes it with what is behind (normal, multiply, screen, overlay, darken, lighten, add) and `opacity(0.6)` makes the whole layer see-through.

## Gradients
Anywhere a fill or stroke color goes you can give a gradient: `rect((0, 0), (480, 200), linear((0, 0), (0, 200), [#f4d35e, #3d1c4f]))` or `circle(c, 80, radial(c, 80, [#fff3c4, #e0607a]))`. Stops are colors, `[t, color]` pairs (t from 0 to 1) or `hard(color)` for a sharp edge; a last argument of 2 to 64 makes flat bands. `gradient(stops, angle)` and `radial_gradient(stops)` fit each shape's own box instead of canvas positions, so one value can be reused on many shapes.

## Pens
`brush(points, pressures, color, pen)` draws a stroke whose width follows the pressure (one number 0 to 1 for each point). The pens are `pens.ink`, `pens.pencil`, `pens.marker`, `pens.brush` and `pens.calligraphy` (all in `pens.list`). A pen is a hash, so you can make your own: `{"name": "mine", "min": 1, "max": 8, "taper": 0.3, "opacity": [1, 1], "nib": null, "grain": 0}`.

## Working with the tools
1. `run` checks the code fast (errors with line and column, what it printed, how many shapes).
2. `render` gives you the picture, so you can see what you drew. Judge it and improve it.
3. `save` writes the .lzdraw into the user's drawings folder (the Linkz editor opens it), `open` reads one back, `svg` gives the SVG text.
4. A drawing may take 2 million steps at most (loops and calls); keep loops small.

## The drawing functions
(Optional parameters, like steps in linear, may be left out. Call docs with a name for one function. Variables you can use: canvas, drawing (the list of shapes), pens, math, text, list.)

blend(mode)
  Sets how the layer it is in mixes with what is behind it.
  mode: "normal", "multiply", "screen", "overlay", "darken", "lighten" or "add"
  example: blend("multiply")

brush(points, pressures, color, pen)
  Draws a smooth curve whose width and opacity follow the pressure of the pen that drew it. The raw pressures are kept, so a different pen restyles the same stroke. The list may also hold curve items like path() does (["c", c1, c2, p] and ["q", c, p]): they are drawn exactly, and the width between two points follows the curve smoothly. There is one pressure for each point or curve item (each ends at one on-curve point), so a curve item takes the pressure at its end. The taper and stamps follow the curves too.
  points: the spots the curve goes through, a list of points and curve items
  pressures: one number from 0 to 1 for each point or curve item
  color: the color of the ink
  pen: a pen style such as pens.ink, pens.pencil or pens.calligraphy
  example: brush([(40, 300), ["c", (80, 200), (200, 200), (260, 240)]], [0.2, 0.8], #1d1d1f, pens.ink)

circle(center, r, fill)
  Draws a filled circle.
  center: the middle of the circle, a point
  r: the radius in pixels
  fill: the color inside
  example: circle((256, 256), 40, #3fa34d)

ellipse(center, radii, fill)
  Draws a filled ellipse.
  center: the middle of the ellipse, a point
  radii: half the width and half the height, a point like (60, 30)
  fill: the color inside
  example: ellipse((256, 256), (60, 30), #e0a526)

gradient(stops, angle, steps)
  A gradient that fits each shape it is given to, across the shape's bounding box. The angle is the direction the colors travel, in screen space, turning clockwise from "to the right": 0deg is left to right, 90deg is top to bottom (the default), 180deg right to left, 270deg bottom to top. This is not CSS: CSS counts from "up", so CSS 180deg is this 90deg. The first stop is at the box's start corner and the last at the opposite corner, so the box is fully covered. Resolved against the path's bounds when the shape is drawn.
  stops: colors, [t, color] pairs or hard(color), at least two
  angle: the direction, like 90deg, 45deg or 0.25turn
  steps: 0 for smooth, or 2 to 64 for that many flat bands
  example: let dusk = gradient([#3d1c4f, #e0607a, #f4d35e])

hard(color)
  Marks a stop as an edge: its color starts right at its place instead of blending from the stop before.
  color: the color after the edge
  example: linear((0, 0), (200, 0), [#f4d35e, #ee964b, hard(#e0607a), #3d1c4f])

line(a, b, color, width)
  Draws a straight line with round ends.
  a: where the line starts, a point
  b: where the line ends, a point
  color: the color of the line
  width: the thickness in pixels
  example: line((20, 100), (380, 100), #1d1d1f, 2)

linear(from, to, stops, steps)
  A gradient that runs along a line, from one point to another.
  from: where the first stop is, a point
  to: where the last stop is, a point
  stops: colors, [t, color] pairs or hard(color), at least two
  steps: 0 for smooth, or 2 to 64 for that many flat bands
  example: rect((0, 0), (200, 100), linear((0, 0), (200, 0), [#f4d35e, #3d1c4f]))

opacity(x)
  Sets how see-through the layer it is in is: 1 is solid, 0 is invisible.
  x: a number from 0 to 1
  example: opacity(0.8)

path(points, fill, closed, smooth, holes, corner)
  Draws a filled shape with a smooth outline, and holes if you give them. The outline is a curve through the points; a point where the line turns by more than `corner` degrees stays a sharp corner, and the pieces between two sharp corners are straight. It is what a traced picture is made of. The list may also hold curve items, drawn exactly (no smoothing through them, and SVG gets real C and Q commands): ["c", c1, c2, p] is a cubic from the point before it to p with controls c1 and c2, ["q", c, p] a quadratic. The first item must be a point. Plain points between two curve items are smoothed as usual, with the points next to a curve as sharp ends.
  points: the outline, a list of points and curve items
  fill: the color inside
  closed: true to join the last point to the first (needed for holes)
  smooth: false for straight sides, like polygon
  holes: a list of such lists, each one cut out of the shape
  corner: the turn in degrees from which a point stays sharp
  example: path([(40, 100), ["c", (40, 20), (160, 20), (160, 100)], (100, 160)], #3fa34d)

polygon(points, fill)
  Draws a filled shape with straight sides.
  points: the corners in order, a list of points
  fill: the color inside
  example: polygon([(100, 20), (180, 120), (20, 120)], #c0392b)

radial(center, r, stops, steps)
  A gradient that runs outwards from a point, as circles.
  center: where the first stop is, a point
  r: the distance where the last stop is, in pixels
  stops: colors, [t, color] pairs or hard(color), at least two
  steps: 0 for smooth, or 2 to 64 for that many flat rings
  example: circle((100, 100), 80, radial((100, 100), 80, [#fff3c4, #e0607a]))

radial_gradient(stops, center, r, steps)
  A gradient that runs outwards from a point of each shape, as circles. The center is a point in fractions of the box ((0, 0) top left, (1, 1) bottom right), and r is a fraction of the box's larger side, so the default r = 0.5 reaches the edge on the longer side. The rings are circles, not an ellipse, because the host evaluates circles only; on a wide box the short sides are not reached. Resolved against the path's bounds when drawn.
  stops: colors, [t, color] pairs or hard(color), at least two
  center: where the first stop is, as fractions of the box
  r: where the last stop is, as a fraction of the larger side
  steps: 0 for smooth, or 2 to 64 for that many flat rings
  example: let glow = radial_gradient([#fff3c4, #e0607a])

rect(pos, size, fill)
  Draws a filled rectangle.
  pos: the top-left corner, a point
  size: width and height, a point like (120, 60)
  fill: the color inside
  example: rect((20, 20), (120, 60), #2d6a8f)

stroke(points, color, width)
  Draws a smooth curve that passes through every point. One point is a dot and two are a straight line. The ends are round.
  points: the spots the curve goes through, a list of points
  color: the color of the line
  width: the thickness in pixels
  example: stroke([(40, 300), (120, 210), (260, 240), (380, 120)], #1d1d1f, 4)
